home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Fredericton: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Fredericton: 4 licensed organizations, local prices, New Brunswick rebates and what 66% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 4 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Fredericton. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Fredericton houses, and which New Brunswick rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Fredericton homes
sections.html:
Of Fredericton's 18,140 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Fredericton house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Fredericton gets about 4,481 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Fredericton. That's about 14% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Fredericton area, 31% of households heat mainly with a heat pump and 30% with electric baseboards; electricity is the main heating energy for 43% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.
Through the Total Home Energy Savings Program, a Certified Energy Advisor charges $99 + HST, covering both the initial and final evaluations.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. Through the Total Home Energy Savings Program, a Certified Energy Advisor charges $99 + HST, covering both the initial and final evaluations.

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Fredericton: sizing a heat pump for −23.3°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Fredericton homes, sized to the local −23.3°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −23.3°C for Fredericton, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Fredericton.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Fredericton
sections.html:
−23.3°C is the 24th-coldest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −23.3°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Fredericton area, 31% of households heat mainly with a heat pump and 30% with electric baseboards; electricity is the main heating energy for 43% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

sections.h2: Why Fredericton homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Fredericton gets about 4,481 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Fredericton. On Fredericton's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Fredericton's 18,140 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (23% of Fredericton's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Fredericton: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in Fredericton: Health Canada survey results for the Region 3 region (17% above the guideline), how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 17% of homes tested in the Region 3 health region were above the guideline, and the only way to know about your house is to test it.

glance.sub: the Fredericton, NB (Fredericton CMA) metro area

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 17% of 112 homes tested in the Region 3 health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 18.5% (1 in 5) of houses at or above the guideline for the Fredericton, NB (Fredericton CMA) metro area.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

• NB Lung's Check Out Radon program lends free electronic screening kits, and the province says about one in four New Brunswick homes exceed the guideline.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Fredericton postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: Rules and help in New Brunswick
sections.html:
• New Brunswick applies the 2020 National Building Code, which requires a radon rough-in in new homes.
  • The province lists the Homeowner Repair Program and the Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program (up to $1,500) as possible help with mitigation costs.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Fredericton?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 17% of 112 homes tested in the Region 3 health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 18.5% (1 in 5) of houses at or above the guideline for the Fredericton, NB (Fredericton CMA) metro area. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Fredericton?
faq.a: NB Lung's Check Out Radon program lends free electronic screening kits, and the province says about one in four New Brunswick homes exceed the guideline. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

mold-testing.h1: Mold and air quality testing in Fredericton
mold-testing.title: Mold testing in Fredericton: air quality sampling and finding the moisture source
mold-testing.description: Mold and indoor air quality testing in Fredericton: when sampling is worth $300–$600, why cold winters cause condensation, and how to find an accredited lab.
mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Fredericton homes
sections.html:
Fredericton gets about 4,481 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Fredericton. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mold usually starts in Fredericton houses.

Of Fredericton's 18,140 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Ask any Fredericton tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Fredericton · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in Fredericton?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing in Fredericton: vermiculite, labs and the New Brunswick rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Fredericton, where 66% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs and the New Brunswick rules for renovation.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 12,000 Fredericton houses (66%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Fredericton houses
sections.html:
Of Fredericton's 18,140 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

In New Brunswick, employers and contractors who disturb asbestos-containing material must follow WorkSafeNB's code of practice for working with asbestos.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in Fredericton

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Fredericton?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. In New Brunswick, employers and contractors who disturb asbestos-containing material must follow WorkSafeNB's code of practice for working with asbestos.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Fredericton: which homes are at risk and how to test
lead-paint-testing.description: 23% of Fredericton's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 23% of Fredericton's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 43% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which Fredericton homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Fredericton's 18,140 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

faq.q: Does my Fredericton house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

sections.h2: How testing works in New Brunswick
sections.html: Owners pay: test kits are at Service New Brunswick offices or RPC, the designated provincial lab in Fredericton and Moncton. The province recommends testing for bacteria twice a year and for inorganic contaminants every two years.

• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

Our well water guide.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in New Brunswick?
faq.a: Owners pay: test kits are at Service New Brunswick offices or RPC, the designated provincial lab in Fredericton and Moncton. The province recommends testing for bacteria twice a year and for inorganic contaminants every two years.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: For bacteria, at least once a year and after flooding, heavy rain or well work; many health units recommend more often. Test chemistry when the well is new and every few years after.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Fredericton: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Fredericton: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 2 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Fredericton: no mandatory reporting rule and 2 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Fredericton
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.NB).

• Commercial Buildings Retrofit Program - energy audit and feasibility study incentives (NB Power (SaveEnergyNB)): ASHRAE Level II audit: 50% of cost up front, max $1,100 (under 15,000 sq ft), $2,200 (15,000-75,000 sq ft) or $3,300 (over 75,000 sq ft); rises to 100% of audit cost, max $3,000 / $5,000 / $8,000 (including the first payment), once one or more recommended measures are done. Feasibility study (instead of a full audit): 100% of cost up to $1,100 / $2,200 / $3,300 when the measure is implemented. Upgrade incentives: $120/GJ for electricity-saving projects (up to $250,000 per fiscal year) and 25% for non-electric upgrades (capped at $1 million per entity). Details
  • Free Energy Walk-Through Service (NB Power (SaveEnergyNB)): Free site visit by a Technical Energy Advisor to find energy-saving projects and matching rebates. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Fredericton buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: We found no mandatory reporting rule for Fredericton buildings as of September 28, 2026.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Fredericton?
faq.a: Yes: Commercial Buildings Retrofit Program - energy audit and feasibility study incentives; Free Energy Walk-Through Service. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
